units.title: The Mystery of Consciousness
units.sub: The brain is an organ you can see; the felt world of “I” is an inner world no one else can see.

share.v: I will give thanks to you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made. Your works are wonderful. My soul knows that very well.

blocks.h: Right now you are reading this line. On the screen there are only tiny points of light, yet you “get” the meaning, and you know that you are reading.

The smell of coffee, the colors of a sunset, the ache of missing someone: all of these are experienced from the inside. Others can measure your heartbeat, but no one can feel it for you. This felt inner world is what we call consciousness.
The spirit of man is Yahweh’s lamp, searching all his innermost parts.
The easy problems and the hard problem
The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons, linked in an extraordinarily complex network. Scientists can already measure which brain regions are active when we see red or hear a sound.

In 1995 the Australian philosopher David Chalmers pointed out that explaining how the brain recognizes and integrates information and controls behavior is the set of “easy problems” (which are not easy at all). The truly “hard problem” is this: why are these physical processes accompanied by subjective experience?

A thermometer can measure exactly 38 °C, yet it does not “feel hot.” A camera can capture a rose, yet it does not “find it beautiful.” Here lies the mystery of consciousness: between processing information and actually feeling something stands a door we still cannot see through.

As early as 1974 the American philosopher Thomas Nagel asked, “What is it like to be a bat?” We could understand everything about a bat’s echolocation and still not know what it experiences from the inside. Subjective experience seems impossible to exhaust with third-person descriptions alone.

Scientists have proposed many theories of consciousness. In 2025 the journal Nature published a large “adversarial collaboration”: supporters of the two leading theories (Global Neuronal Workspace Theory and Integrated Information Theory) preregistered their predictions, which were then tested with fMRI, MEG and intracranial electrodes in 256 participants. Key predictions of both theories failed to find support. This is not failure but honest progress: consciousness remains a frontier of science.
Let’s look at each claim separately and mark how certain it is.
The human brain has roughly 86 billion neurons.
States of consciousness (waking, sleep, anesthesia) are closely tied to brain activity; brain damage changes conscious experience.
There is currently no agreed theory of how the brain produces subjective experience; the leading theories were not fully supported in the 2025 adversarial test.

Subjective experience is very hard to reduce entirely to the workings of matter. That makes the view that “the mind is real” worth taking seriously, and a personal Creator who is himself spirit naturally explains why conscious minds appear in the universe. Even Nagel, an atheist, argued in 2012 that the materialist account is “almost certainly false.”
Perspectives Room
What exactly is consciousness? Here are two major views side by side.

items.h: Consciousness is entirely brain activity. Daniel Dennett and others argue that so-called irreducible “qualia” are a misunderstanding, and that future neuroscience will eventually explain consciousness.

Subjective experience is a real, irreplaceable dimension that physical description cannot fully capture. Theists hold that the mind comes from God, who is himself spirit; some non-theists propose other options, such as panpsychism.

blocks.h: He placed a “spirit” within us
The Bible says that human beings are not just dust; they also have the breath of life that comes from God.
Yahweh God formed man from the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
That you can feel, reflect and know that “I” exist is itself a gift. Inside every person is a world others cannot see, known only to their own spirit and to God.
For who among men knows the things of a man, except the spirit of the man, which is in him? Even so, no one knows the things of God, except God’s Spirit.
Be still for one minute and notice that you are “aware”: your breathing, the sounds around you, the thoughts in your heart. The you who is aware was made by God’s own hand.
Reflect: Do I treat myself as nothing more than a machine that works, forgetting that I have a soul that needs God?

Prayer: Lord who made me, thank you for giving me a mind that can feel, think and know you. Let your lamp shine into every corner of my inner life, and turn my heart wholly toward you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Holy Spirit is my guide: the spirit of man is the Lord’s lamp. Each day, be still for a moment and let the Holy Spirit shine into my heart.
Humility overcomes pride: if I cannot even fully explain my own consciousness, I admit that I am limited and let God be God.
People matter more than tasks: everyone around me has an unseen inner world worth respecting; they are not tools for getting work done.

blocks.h: This week: find a family member or friend and, without rushing to give advice, listen closely for ten minutes as they share what they are feeling.

quiz.e: The hard problem is not how the brain processes information, but why there is any “feeling” at all.

o: Key predictions of both theories were partly unsupported
Integrated Information Theory was fully confirmed

quiz.e: Both theories ran into challenges; consciousness remains a scientific frontier.

quiz.q: According to Genesis 2:7, how did man become “a living soul”?
o: He gradually awakened on his own
He ate fruit from the tree of life
God breathed into his nostrils the breath of life
quiz.e: Human life and the human spirit both come from God.

units.title: Can We Trust Reason?
units.sub: We use reason to think about everything, but why should reason itself be trusted?

share.v: The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.

blocks.h: Someone says, “I don’t trust any reasoning.” But in saying so, he is reasoning. Even to doubt reason, you must first trust reason.

Even more astonishing, the universe can be understood by human minds. In 1936 Einstein wrote that the eternal mystery of the world is its comprehensibility. (The popular version, “The most incomprehensible thing about the universe is that it is comprehensible,” is a paraphrase.)
The fear of Yahweh is the beginning of knowledge, but the foolish despise wisdom and instruction.
Two remarkable “just so” facts

First, the human mind can grasp logic and mathematics. Second, the universe actually runs according to mathematics. In 1960 the Nobel Prize–winning physicist Eugene Wigner called this “the unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences,” and described it as “a wonderful gift which we neither understand nor deserve.”

Imagine sitting in a room and drawing a map with nothing but pencil and paper. You step outside and find that the mountains and rivers match your map at every point. That is often how it goes with mathematics: structures worked out on paper are later found to describe nature exactly.

For example, in 1928 Paul Dirac wrote down an equation describing the electron. Its solutions implied the existence of a positively charged “anti-electron.” In 1932 Carl Anderson actually found the positron in cosmic rays.

In Miracles, C. S. Lewis put forward the “argument from reason”: if our thoughts are entirely the product of non-rational causes, we have little reason to believe they are true. In 1948 the philosopher Elizabeth Anscombe pointed out flaws in his argument; Lewis humbly accepted the criticism and rewrote Chapter 3 for the revised 1960 edition. That itself is a fine example of intellectual honesty.

The contemporary philosopher Alvin Plantinga proposed the “evolutionary argument against naturalism”: natural selection favors behavior that helps survival, not necessarily beliefs that are true. If naturalism (no God) and evolution are both true, the probability that our cognitive faculties are reliable is low or impossible to assess, so the naturalist loses any guarantee even for his own reasoning. His conclusion: the real conflict is not between science and faith but between science and naturalism.
Mathematics has astonishing predictive power in physics; for example, the Dirac equation predicted the positron, which was discovered later.
Natural selection preserves cognitive abilities that aid survival, but scholars still debate how “aiding survival” relates to “seeing the truth.”

The reliability of reason and the intelligibility of the universe both point to a rational Creator, who made human beings in his image and made the universe with a rational order. This is a philosophical inference.
Perspectives Room

items.h: Philosophers such as Fitelson & Sober argue that Plantinga’s probability reasoning is flawed; others argue that true beliefs usually aid survival, so evolution is enough to explain why reason is broadly reliable.
Even if true beliefs often aid survival, this still assumes a world with a stable, intelligible order. Theism holds that mind and universe come from the same wise God, so their fit is no coincidence.

blocks.h: A mind made in God’s image
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

Many early scientists believed the universe has order because the God who made it is faithful, and that humans can understand the universe because they are made in God’s image. Reason is not the enemy of faith; it is God’s gift for knowing the truth.
You will know the truth, and the truth will make you free.
Think of what you have used reason for today: balancing accounts, making plans, understanding a paragraph. Every act of thinking is using a gift from God.
Reflect: Do I use reason to seek the truth, or to find excuses for what I already want to do?
Prayer: God of wisdom, thank you for giving me a mind that can think. Renew my mind, so that my reason bows to your truth and is lit by your Word. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: reason is a good tool, and God’s Word is the measuring line. Let my thinking happen in the light of Scripture.
Changing our mindset changes our lives: from “information” to “revelation,” ask the Holy Spirit to turn head knowledge into heart conviction.
Humility overcomes pride: the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; the more I learn about the universe, the more I admit my limits.

blocks.h: This week: write down one question about faith you have had recently, study a related Bible passage, and talk it through with a spiritual companion.
Quiz

o: The speed of computers

quiz.e: Mathematics worked out on paper often turns out to describe the universe exactly.

quiz.q: How did C. S. Lewis respond to Anscombe’s criticism?
o: He refused to respond
He gave up his faith
He humbly accepted it and rewrote a chapter of the book
quiz.e: He rewrote Chapter 3 in the revised 1960 edition, an example of intellectual honesty.

quiz.q: Where does Plantinga say the real conflict lies?
o: Between science and naturalism
Between science and faith
Between mathematics and physics
quiz.e: He argues that science fits with theistic belief; the conflict is between science and naturalism.

units.title: The Moral Law Written on the Heart
units.sub: A child’s untaught cry of “That’s not fair!” reveals a measuring rule within the heart.

share.v: He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

blocks.h: Two children are splitting a cake, and the younger one immediately shouts, “That’s not fair!” No one ever taught him a definition of fairness, yet he knows a line has been crossed.
C. S. Lewis noticed that when people quarrel, they rarely say, “I’m stronger than you.” They say, “You shouldn’t do that.” Both sides quietly appeal to the same standard.

For when Gentiles who don’t have the law do by nature the things of the law, these, not having the law, are a law to themselves, in that they show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience testifying with them, and their thoughts among themselves accusing or else excusing them.
A morality shared across cultures

In 2019 a research team at the University of Oxford analyzed ethnographic records from 60 societies and found seven cooperative behaviors regarded as good in the societies studied: helping family, helping your group, returning favors, courage, deference to superiors, dividing resources fairly, and respecting others’ property. They found no society that regarded these behaviors as bad; cultures differed only in how they ranked them.

The world’s musical styles vary endlessly, yet they are all built on a few shared intervals and rhythms. Morality is like that: each culture plays a different tune, but beneath them lies the same “scale.”

In Book One of Mere Christianity, C. S. Lewis argues that the moral law is not merely instinct, because when two instincts clash (the urge to help someone and the urge to protect yourself), something inside tells us which one to follow. Nor is it merely social convention, because we say that one society’s morality is better than another’s, which means there is a standard higher than every society.

A 2007 experiment reported that infants aged 6 to 10 months preferred a “helper” puppet over a “hinderer” puppet. But a large 2025 replication across 37 laboratories with 567 infants did not reproduce this preference. We should not present a single study as settled fact.
In ethnographies of 60 societies, seven cooperative behaviors were widely regarded as good; the researchers note that more detailed tests with new data are still needed.
Whether infants are born making moral evaluations is currently unclear: the original study reported a preference, but a large replication failed to reproduce it.
If there is a universal, objective moral law binding on everyone, the best explanation is a good Lawgiver. This is C. S. Lewis’s famous moral argument.
Perspectives Room
Where do moral intuitions come from? Can they tell us what is truly right and wrong? Here are two major views side by side.

items.h: Moral intuitions may be products of evolution that promote cooperation. The philosopher Sharon Street goes further: if so, we have little reason to believe our moral intuitions reflect objective moral truth.

Evolution can explain “how” we came to have a moral sense, but not that “harming the innocent really is wrong.” If morality is only a survival strategy, that statement loses its real weight, a conclusion most people cannot accept. Theism provides a foundation for objective morality.

blocks.h: A righteous God writes his law on human hearts
Paul says that even people without the law have a conscience bearing witness within them. This standard was not invented by humans; it was engraved by the God who made us.
He has shown you, O man, what is good. What does Yahweh require of you, but to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with your God?

Yet knowing what is good is not the same as doing it. Every one of us has gone against the standard in our own hearts. This standard points not only to a Lawgiver; it also shows us that we need salvation.
Recall a moment when seeing injustice made your heart burn. That righteous anger reflects God’s righteous character.
Reflect: I measure others strictly by the standard in my heart. Am I just as honest when I measure myself?

Prayer: Righteous and good God, thank you for writing your law on my heart. Forgive me where I have knowingly done wrong, and give me strength to act justly, to love mercy, and to walk humbly with you. In Jesus’ name, Amen.
321 Life Application

items: The Bible is my standard: conscience needs to be calibrated by God’s Word; let Scripture be my final standard of right and wrong.
920 (living out the ninefold fruit of the Spirit): morality is not just rules but living out the Spirit’s fruit of goodness, faithfulness and gentleness in relationships.
Humility overcomes pride: measure myself with this standard first, then others.
